statement: The rule for a school trip is: "A pupil may go on the trip only if they have returned the form." The rule was followed. Rina went on the trip, and Sam returned the form. Which of these must be true?

choices.misconception: I read "only if" as "if", so I thought returning the form is enough to go, but it is only needed.

choices.text: Sam did not go on the trip.
choices.misconception: I thought the rule stops Sam from going, but it only says the form is needed, and Sam has returned it.

choices.text: Nothing can be said about Rina.
choices.misconception: I thought the rule only talks about the form, so it tells us nothing for sure about someone who went.

choices.text: Everyone who returned the form went on the trip.
choices.misconception: I turned the rule around, but returning the form does not make anyone go.

hints: Could a pupil who had not returned the form go on the trip?
An "only if" rule names something every pupil who goes must have done. It does not say that doing it is enough to go. Test each choice: must it be true, or only could it be true?
Rina went, so she must have returned the form. Sam returned the form, but that does not tell us whether he went.

solutions.reliable: The rule says nobody goes on the trip without returning the form. Rina went, so she must have returned the form. Sam returned the form, but the rule does not say that everyone who returns the form goes, so Sam may or may not have gone; neither "Sam went" nor "Sam did not go" must be true. For the same reason, "everyone who returned the form went" is not certain. The transferable idea: "A only if B" means every A has B, and nothing more.

whyOnTest: Reading "only if" precisely, as a condition that is needed but not enough, is the core of logic questions on the test.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
